In SEO and adjacent web practice, there is a recurring error in thinking: consent is treated as a decorative banner rather than as part of the site’s actual architecture. As a result, the market easily slides into crude formulas like “no banner means non-compliance.” For a professional discussion, that is far too simplistic.

- If you look at a site as a system, the primary issue is not the banner but the load map: analytics, GTM, pixels, video embeds, maps, reCAPTCHA, booking widgets, external forms, and any mechanisms that access the device before consent. Without this inventory, it is impossible to speak honestly either about compliance or about the technical correctness of the implementation.
- For SEO, this is not an abstraction either. Any external script is not only a legal object but also an infrastructure object: performance, loading order, control over third-party dependencies, the impact of tag management on data collection, and the risk of false conclusions by the site owner. Consent logic is part of the technical model, not just legal UX.
- I believe one more distinction matters. Good-faith consulting states the conditions clearly: with one configuration, a CMP is required; with another, it is not, but a privacy section is still mandatory. Bad practice presents this as a universal threat. What breaks here is not only ethics, but also the precision of professional language.

In your own practice, how do you check consent-relevant technologies: through a manual audit, through a crawler/scanner, or through a combination of code, network, and tag review?
